strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: The paper bridges the gap between spatial 3D scene graphs and functional 3D scene graphs by proposing a Unified 3DSG representation that jointly captures objects, interactive parts, spatial relations, functional relations, and affordances.

Well-engineered and principled framework: The proposed pipeline directly tackles key bottlenecks in 3D part-level perception, including knowledge-guided part candidate generation, color-distribution feature integration to stabilize multi-view 3D part association, and geometry-anchored multi-agent LLM reasoning that prevents combinatorial explosion and hallucinations.

Valuable benchmark contribution: The UniGraph3D benchmark consolidates and canonicalizes existing noisy datasets (FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D), providing standardized annotations for object-part relations, multi-level spatial/functional edges, and affordances.

Comprehensive experimental validation: OP3DSG demonstrates large quantitative improvements over existing open-vocabulary baselines (e.g., +31.2% R@3 on part nodes, substantial gains on functional/spatial triplets). Ablation studies isolate the impact of individual design components, and real-world deployment on a Stretch3 robot illustrates practical utility.
weaknesses: Generalizability and true open-vocabulary nature of the knowledge base: The object-part candidate generation stage relies on a pre-curated knowledge base $K$ covering common indoor object-part relations. It remains unclear how robust the system is to novel or rare objects outside of $K$, and whether dynamic querying of an LLM for $K(c)$ would preserve efficiency and accuracy.

Part localization accuracy under strict geometric metrics: As shown in Table 4, part node localization under IoU $\ge$ 0.10 (25.8%) and IoP $\ge$ 0.25 (13.0%) drops significantly compared to loose recall, and trails KeySG on IoP (23.4%). This indicates that precise 3D bounding box estimation for small components remains a persistent challenge in surface-based fusion.

Heuristic rigidity in prior graph construction: The intra-object association in the prior graph relies on simple spatial proximity (< 1 meter) and string containment heuristics (e.g., the object label being a substring of the part label). This could fail for non-compound part labels or spatially extensive furniture where centers are more than 1 meter apart.

Lack of quantitative evaluation for downstream robotic tasks: While Section 6 illustrates real-world robotic applications (question answering, task planning, navigation), the evaluation remains purely qualitative. Reporting quantitative task success rates or comparative efficiency against prior 3DSG backbones would significantly strengthen the robotic claims.

strengths: Compelling formulation that bridges the gap between spatial and functional 3D scene graphs, providing a unified representation (objects, parts, spatial relations, functional relations, and affordances) critical for fine-grained embodied AI tasks.

Well-engineered architecture addressing known failure modes of foundation models in part perception: combining knowledge-guided candidate expansion, color-distribution features to assist multi-view part fusion, and geometry-anchored multi-agent LLM reasoning to avoid O(N^2) scaling issues.

Comprehensive benchmark contribution (UniGraph3D) that resolves annotation ambiguities in existing datasets (FunGraph3D, SceneFun3D) and introduces explicit part-level spatial and affordance annotations.
Significant quantitative improvements over adapted competitive baselines across node retrieval, relational triplet recall, and affordance prediction, backed by detailed ablation studies.
Practical demonstration of real-world applicability on a mobile manipulator (Stretch3) across question answering, task planning, and goal-directed navigation.
weaknesses: The open-vocabulary claim is partially constrained by reliance on a pre-curated object-part knowledge base K to expand part candidates; the paper would benefit from detailing the scale/breadth of K and discussing failure modes when encountering novel objects or unconventional part hierarchies not covered by K.

Part localization accuracy under strict geometric metrics remains relatively modest (Table 4 reports 25.8% for part IoU >= 0.10 and 13.0% for IoP >= 0.25), indicating that the main retrieval metric (non-zero 3D IoU) is quite lenient and can obscure 3D bounding box misalignment or noise in surface fusion.

Computational overhead and run-time efficiency of the multi-agent LLM pipeline and multi-view color feature computation are not sufficiently discussed or benchmarked against standard real-time or streaming requirements.

strengths: Well-motivated unified formulation: Combining object-centric spatial scene graphs and part-centric functional scene graphs into a unified representation addresses a clear and important gap for embodied AI and physical scene understanding.

Tractable reasoning architecture: The use of a geometry-initialized prior graph and decomposed LLM agents (local, remote, affordance) effectively curbs the quadratic explosion of candidate relations that arises when fine-grained parts are introduced as graph nodes.

Comprehensive benchmark contribution: The UniGraph3D benchmark consolidates and disambiguates previous fragmented datasets (FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D) by providing unified annotations across object-part spatial hierarchies, functional relations, and affordances.

Solid empirical evaluation and ablation: The paper evaluates multiple baselines across both GPT-4 and updated model variants, performs detailed ablation studies validating the individual components (knowledge prior, color features, prior graph, agent decomposition), and showcases a functional real-robot demonstration on a Stretch3 platform.
weaknesses: Open-vocabulary claims constrained by predefined knowledge base: The part-level detection heavily relies on an empirically curated object-part knowledge dictionary K to inject part prompts. While effective for common indoor objects, this heuristic restricts true open-world generalization to novel or unseen compositional objects.

Weak 3D part localization accuracy under stricter metrics: The localization sensitivity analysis in Table 4 reveals that part node IoU drops sharply to 25.8% at IoU >= 0.10 and 13.0% at IoP >= 0.25. Given that interactive parts (e.g., knobs, handles) require centimeter-level spatial precision for physical robot manipulation, this remains a significant practical bottleneck.

Permissive overlap criterion in main benchmarks: The main evaluations in Tables 2 and 3 adopt a non-zero 3D IoU criterion for node matching. This threshold is quite lenient and can award matches to loose or imprecise bounding boxes, potentially inflating recall figures.

Qualitative-only robotic evaluation: While the deployment on the Hello Robot Stretch3 demonstrates end-to-end integration across QA, task planning, and navigation, Section 6 lacks quantitative success rates, execution speeds, and failure analysis for physical interaction trials.

strengths: Unifying spatial and functional 3D scene graphs into a coherent representation with objects, parts, spatial/functional relations, and affordances addresses a crucial bottleneck in fine-grained scene understanding for embodied AI.

The technical design thoughtfully targets the specific challenges of part-level 3DSGs: using object-part knowledge priors to mitigate open-vocabulary part detection failure, multi-space color histograms to improve small-part multi-view 3D association, and a geometry-initialized prior graph to bound LLM reasoning space.
The introduction of UniGraph3D provides a well-motivated, consolidated benchmark that resolves label ambiguities and inconsistencies present in prior datasets (SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D).

Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (UniGraph3D, ReplicaSSG, per-dataset splits) and clear ablations demonstrate substantial performance and efficiency improvements over competitive baselines.

The real-world robotic demonstration on the Stretch3 robot highlights the practical feasibility of the generated scene graphs across downstream embodied tasks (QA, text-query navigation, task planning).
weaknesses: The part proposal stage relies on a manually curated object-part knowledge base K to generate candidates; the extent to which this limits generalization to arbitrary open-vocabulary objects or out-of-distribution environments is not fully analyzed.

As shown in Table 4, part localization accuracy under stricter overlap criteria (IoU >= 0.10, IoP >= 0.25) remains relatively low, indicating that accurate 3D spatial boundary estimation for fine-grained parts remains challenging.

The real-world robot demonstrations across question answering, navigation, and task planning are evaluated primarily qualitatively as proof-of-concept demonstrations rather than through standardized quantitative task success metrics.

strengths: Compelling formulation and unification: Bridging the gap between object-centric spatial 3D scene graphs and functional 3D scene graphs by jointly modeling objects, actionable parts, spatial/functional relations, and affordances is well-motivated and impactful for embodied AI.

Well-designed, modular framework: The proposed pipeline addresses core bottlenecks effectively—leveraging object-part knowledge to guide part detection, integrating color-distribution features to stabilize part association across views, and utilizing a geometry-initialized prior graph with multi-agent LLM reasoning to scale relation prediction without dense, computationally expensive VLM captioning.

Comprehensive benchmark: UniGraph3D consolidates existing fragmented functional datasets, cleans up ambiguous relation labels into canonical forms, and adds explicit spatial relation and affordance annotations, establishing a solid testbed for future research.

Strong empirical results and efficiency: OP3DSG demonstrates substantial gains in both node recall (especially part nodes by >30%) and relation recall over established baselines, alongside reduced GPU memory footprint and fewer model invocations.
Real-world demonstration: The paper validates the approach on a physical mobile manipulator (Stretch3) across multiple downstream embodied tasks including QA, navigation, and task planning.
weaknesses: Open-vocabulary limitations imposed by the knowledge base: The framework uses a pre-curated object-part knowledge base $\mathcal{K}$ to expand part candidates. While this mitigates missed parts, it somewhat limits the true 'open-vocabulary' generality of part discovery when confronting rare or out-of-distribution objects with atypical parts.

Low geometric precision for part nodes: As revealed in the localization sensitivity analysis (Table 4), the part node retrieval drops significantly when strict 3D IoU/IoP thresholds are applied (e.g., 25.8% at IoU $\ge$ 0.10). The geometric fidelity of small parts in fused 3D space remains a challenge.

Qualitative-only robot evaluation: The downstream robotics tasks in Section 6 and Figure 5 are presented as qualitative demonstrations. Including quantitative task success rates (e.g., success rate and path length efficiency for navigation and planning compared to baseline representations) would have provided stronger empirical backing for embodied utility.
Scale of UniGraph3D: Although the benchmark curation is valuable, the overall scale (251 object nodes and 414 part nodes across the consolidated scenes) remains relatively modest.

strengths: Unification of Spatial and Functional 3DSGs: The paper addresses an important and timely gap in 3D scene understanding by formulating the Unified 3D Scene Graph, which simultaneously represents objects, actionable parts, spatial relations, functional relations, and physical affordances within a single structured representation.

Well-Motivated Technical Components: The proposed pipeline sensibly tackles key bottlenecks in fine-grained 3D grounding: (1) using an object-part knowledge base to alleviate foundation model neglect of small components, (2) incorporating color-distribution statistics to stabilize part association across views, and (3) constraining LLM reasoning via a geometry-initialized prior graph and modular agents.

Solid Benchmark Contribution: UniGraph3D harmonizes and refines the noisy and inconsistent label spaces of prior datasets (SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D) into canonical relations and unified affordances, providing a valuable testbed for fine-grained 3D reasoning.

Comprehensive Experimental Evaluation and Real-World Demonstration: The paper provides extensive experiments on UniGraph3D, separate evaluations on source datasets, out-of-domain evaluation on ReplicaSSG, detailed component ablations, and a physical demonstration on a Stretch3 robot.
weaknesses: Compromised Open-Vocabulary Flexibility via Curated Knowledge Base: A core motivation is open-vocabulary scene understanding, yet part candidate generation relies on an empirically curated object-part knowledge base K. This inherently restricts the part vocabulary to predetermined pairs and limits generalization to rare, customized, or non-standard objects/parts not covered by the curated base.

Low Geometric Localization Accuracy for Part Nodes: As revealed in Table 4 (Node Localization Sensitivity), OP3DSG achieves only 25.8% Part Node R@3 at IoU >= 0.10 and 13.0% at IoP >= 0.25, underperforming baseline methods like KeySG (30.4% and 23.4%). This indicates that while semantic part classification is strong, precise 3D spatial grounding and bounding-box quality for small parts remain weak.

Heavy Reliance on Hand-Crafted Heuristics: The pipeline contains multiple heuristic engineering rules—such as HSV thresholding for specular rejection, weighting across three distinct color histograms, fixed 1-meter Euclidean thresholds for neighbor candidates, and lexical substring containment matching for intra-object edges. The robustness and sensitivity of these hyperparameters across different environments are not thoroughly analyzed.

Lack of Quantitative Evaluation for Robot Downstream Tasks: While Section 6 demonstrates qualitative execution on a Stretch3 platform across QA, planning, and navigation, no quantitative metrics (e.g., success rate, planning time, task completion rate against baselines) are reported to substantiate the downstream robotics benefits.
